paragraphs: “Gentlemen of the jury, let me remind you that a man’s life is at stake, and that you must be careful. We have heard the prosecutor himself admit that until today he hesitated to accuse the prisoner of full and conscious premeditation of the crime. He hesitated until he saw that fatal drunken letter, which was produced in court today. ‘All was done as written.’ But I repeat: he was running to her, to look for her, solely to find out where she was. That fact cannot be disputed. Had she been at home, he would not have run away. He would have stayed at her side, and so would not have done what he promised in the letter. He ran off unexpectedly and by chance, and by then he very likely did not even remember his drunken letter. ‘He snatched up the pestle,’ they say, and you will remember how a whole edifice of psychology was built on that pestle—why he was bound to see it as a weapon, to snatch it up, and so on and so on. A very commonplace thought occurs to me here. What if that pestle had not been in sight? What if it had not been lying on the shelf from which the prisoner snatched it, but had been put away in a cupboard? It would not have caught his eye, and he would have run off without a weapon, with empty hands, and then he would certainly not have killed anyone. How, then, can I take the pestle as proof of premeditation?

“Yes, but he talked in the taverns of murdering his father. And two days before, on the evening he wrote his drunken letter, he was quiet and only quarreled with a shopman in the tavern—because a Karamazov could not help quarreling, of course! My answer is this. If he was planning such a murder as the letter describes, he certainly would not have quarreled even with a shopman. He probably would not have gone into the tavern at all. A person plotting such a crime looks for quiet and seclusion. He wants to efface himself, to avoid being seen and heard, and he does it not from calculation but from instinct. Gentlemen of the jury, the psychological method is a two-edged weapon, and we can use it too. As for all this shouting in taverns throughout the month, do we not often hear children, or drunkards coming out of taverns, shout, ‘I’ll kill you’? Yet they do not murder anyone. And that fatal letter—is it not simply drunken irritability as well? Is it not simply the shout of a brawler outside a tavern, ‘I’ll kill you! I’ll kill the lot of you!’ Why not? Why could it not be that? What reason have we to call that letter ‘fatal’ rather than absurd? Because his father has been found murdered. Because a witness saw the prisoner running out of the garden with a weapon in his hand, and was knocked down by him. Therefore, we are told, everything was done as he had planned in writing, and the letter was not ‘absurd’ but ‘fatal.’

“Now, thank God, we have come to the real point: ‘Since he was in the garden, he must have murdered him.’ In those few words—‘since he _was_, then he _must_’—lies the whole case for the prosecution. He was there, so he must have done it. And what if there is no _must_ about it, even if he was there? Oh, I admit that the chain of evidence, the coincidences, are truly suggestive. But examine all these facts separately, without regard to their connection. Why, for instance, does the prosecution refuse to accept the prisoner’s statement that he ran away from his father’s window? Remember the sarcasm the prosecutor poured on the respectful and ‘pious’ feelings that suddenly came over the murderer. But what if there was something of the sort—a feeling of religious awe, if not of respect for his father? ‘My mother must have been praying for me at that moment,’ the prisoner said at the preliminary inquiry. And so he ran away as soon as he had convinced himself that Madame Svyetlov was not in his father’s house. ‘But he could not have convinced himself by looking through the window,’ the prosecutor objects. Why could he not? Why? The window opened at the signals the prisoner gave. Fyodor Pavlovitch might have said some word, some exclamation, that showed the prisoner she was not there. Why should we assume everything happened as we imagine it, as we have made up our minds to imagine it? A thousand things may happen in reality that escape the subtlest imagination.

“‘Yes, but Grigory saw the door open, so the prisoner was certainly in the house, and therefore he killed him.’ Now, about that door, gentlemen of the jury.... Note that we have the statement of only one witness about that door, and he was at the time in such a condition that— But suppose the door was open. Suppose the prisoner lied in denying it, out of an instinct of self-defense, natural in his position. Suppose he did go into the house—well, what then? How does it follow that, because he was there, he committed the murder? He might have dashed in and run through the rooms. He might have pushed his father away. He might have struck him. But as soon as he had made sure Madame Svyetlov was not there, he may have run away, rejoicing that she was not there and that he had not killed his father. And it was perhaps just because he had escaped the temptation to kill his father, because he had a clear conscience and was glad he had not killed him, that he was capable of a pure feeling, a feeling of pity and compassion. That is why, a minute later, he leapt off the fence to help Grigory, after he had knocked him down in his excitement.

“With terrible eloquence the prosecutor has described to us the dreadful state of the prisoner’s mind at Mokroe, when love lay before him again, calling him to a new life. Love was impossible for him, said the prosecutor, because he had his father’s bloodstained corpse behind him, and beyond that corpse—retribution. And yet the prosecutor allowed him love, which he explained, according to his method, by talking about his drunken condition, about a criminal being taken to execution, about its still being far off, and so on and so on. But again I ask, Mr. Prosecutor, have you not invented a new personality? Is the prisoner so coarse and heartless that he could think at that moment of love, and of dodges to escape punishment, if his hands were really stained with his father’s blood? No, no, no! As soon as it was made plain to him that she loved him and called him to her side, promising him new happiness, oh, then, I protest, he must have felt the impulse to suicide doubled and trebled. He must have killed himself, if he had his father’s murder on his conscience. Oh, no! He would not have forgotten where his pistols lay! I know the prisoner. The savage, stony heartlessness the prosecutor ascribes to him does not fit his character. He would have killed himself—that is certain. He did not kill himself just because ‘his mother’s prayers had saved him,’ and he was innocent of his father’s blood. He was troubled, he was grieving that night at Mokroe only about old Grigory. He was praying to God that the old man would recover, that his blow had not been fatal, and that he would not have to suffer for it. Why not accept such an interpretation of the facts? What trustworthy proof have we that the prisoner is lying?

“But we shall be told at once again, ‘There is his father’s corpse! If he ran away without murdering him, who did murder him?’ Here, I repeat, you have the whole logic of the prosecution. Who murdered him, if not he? There is no one to put in his place.

“Gentlemen of the jury, is that really so? Is it positively, actually true that there is no one else at all? We heard the prosecutor count on his fingers all the persons who were in that house that night. There were five. Three of them, I agree, could not have been responsible: the murdered man himself, old Grigory, and his wife. That leaves the prisoner and Smerdyakov. And the prosecutor exclaims, with a flourish, that the prisoner pointed to Smerdyakov only because he had no one else to fix on. Had there been a sixth person, he says, even a phantom of a sixth person, the prisoner would have dropped the charge against Smerdyakov at once, in shame, and accused that other. But, gentlemen of the jury, why may I not draw the very opposite conclusion? There are two persons—the prisoner and Smerdyakov. Why can I not say that you accuse my client simply because you have no one else to accuse? And you have no one else only because you have determined to exclude Smerdyakov from all suspicion.

“It is true that Smerdyakov is accused only by the prisoner, his two brothers, and Madame Svyetlov. But there are others who accuse him. There are vague rumors of a question, of a suspicion, an obscure report, a feeling of expectation. Finally, we have the evidence of a combination of facts that is very suggestive, though, I admit, inconclusive. In the first place, there is the fit that came on precisely on the day of the catastrophe. For some reason the prosecutor has felt obliged to defend its genuineness with great care. Then there is Smerdyakov’s sudden suicide on the eve of the trial. Then there is the equally startling evidence given in court today by the elder of the prisoner’s brothers. He had believed in the prisoner’s guilt, but today he produced a bundle of notes and proclaimed Smerdyakov the murderer. Oh, I fully share the conviction of the court and the prosecutor that Ivan Karamazov is suffering from brain fever. His statement may really be a desperate effort, planned in delirium, to save his brother by throwing the guilt on the dead man. But still Smerdyakov’s name is spoken, and again there is a suggestion of mystery. There is something unexplained, incomplete. And perhaps it may one day be explained. But we will not go into that now. That is for later.
